quiz.title: IP Quiz
theory.address.binaryNote: The bar sits on the /19 boundary. Left of it are the 19 network bits — identical in every row, which is what the AND preserves. Right of it are the 13 host bits, and they are the only difference between the two results: all 0 gives the network address, all 1 gives the broadcast address. Everything in between is a usable host.
theory.hostCount.binaryNote: Only the 8 digits right of the bar can change, and 8 bits have 2^8 = 256 combinations. Two of them are spoken for — 00000000 is the network address, 11111111 the broadcast address — which leaves 254. Note that the address itself, 11101010 in the last octet, never enters the calculation.
theory.split.binaryNote: The three S bits were host bits before the split; borrowing them moved the boundary three places to the right. They simply count up — 000, 001, 010 … 111 — which is why there are exactly eight subnets and why the third octet steps in 32s: those three bits carry the values 128, 64 and 32.
theory.mask.binaryNote: Count the ones and you have the prefix; there is nothing else to a mask. They always come in one run, and everything after them is zeros. The last row breaks that rule — after a zero another one appears, 10100000 — so 255.255.255.160 is not a mask at all.
theory.address.worked3: Network value from the host octet
theory.address.thought1: 255 means the whole octet belongs to the network and 0 means the whole octet is free — neither tells you anything. The one octet in between is where the boundary actually falls, so that is the one you work with.
theory.address.thought3: The networks start at 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160 and so on. You need the last one at or below 128. Dividing 128 by 32 gives 4 with nothing left over, so 128 is itself the start of a block — the fifth one.
theory.address.thought4: The next network starts at 160, so the last address still belonging to ours is the one immediately before it. In the octet after it, everything is set to its maximum, which is 255.
theory.hostCount.thought2: Every one of the 8 bits is independent and can be 0 or 1. Two possibilities for the first, doubled by the second, doubled again by the third, and so on eight times over.
theory.hostCount.thought3: These two are not free to hand out: one names the network itself, the other addresses everyone in it at once. Every other combination is a host.
theory.split.thought1: Equally sized subnets only come in powers of two, so count them out: 2^1 is 2, not enough for 5. 2^2 is 4, still not enough. 2^3 is 8, and 8 is enough. So you make 8 subnets and simply leave the three you do not need unused.
theory.split.thought2: The exponent is the number of bits: 8 subnets came from 2³, so 3 bits. Those 3 bits are exactly what you take from the host part.
theory.mask.thought2: The 2 leftover bits are the leftmost ones of the octet, and the leftmost bits carry the largest values: 128 and 64, which add up to 192. The shortcut 256 − 2^(8 − r) says the same thing in one step.
theory.address.title: Network and broadcast address
theory.address.intro: Two methods get you there: a binary AND, or the block size. Go binary when the prefix is unfamiliar, use the block size when you want to be quick.
theory.address.step1: Find the interesting octet: the first octet of the mask that is neither 255 nor 0.
theory.address.step2: Block size = 256 − that octet of the mask.
theory.address.step3: The largest multiple of the block size that is less than or equal to the host octet is the network value.
theory.address.step4: The broadcast address is the one address before the next block starts.
theory.address.note: Usable hosts = 2^(32 − prefix) − 2; the network and broadcast addresses do not count. In binary you can read it straight off: the network bits stay as they are, host bits all 0 give the network address and all 1 give the broadcast address.
theory.hostCount.title: Usable host addresses
theory.hostCount.intro: The count depends on the prefix alone. Which address the question shows makes no difference to the answer — it only tells you which network you are in.
theory.hostCount.step2: Every combination of those bits is one address, so the network holds 2^host bits addresses.
theory.hostCount.step3: Two of them are taken: all host bits 0 is the network address, all 1 is the broadcast address.
theory.hostCount.note: 192.168.252.234/24 and 10.0.0.1/24 both have 254 usable addresses. The exceptions are /31 (point-to-point, RFC 3021) and /32 (a single host route), where the formula would give 0 and −1.
theory.split.title: Splitting a network into subnets
theory.split.intro: Equally sized subnets only come in powers of two: you borrow bits from the host part, and those bits lengthen the prefix.
theory.split.step1: Round the number of subnets you need up to the next power of two.
theory.split.step2: 2^n is that number, so you borrow n bits.
theory.split.step4: The new networks follow one block size apart, starting at the original network.
theory.split.note: Two common traps: the new networks carry the new prefix (/19, not /16), and counting starts at the first block — the first subnet is 192.168.0.0/19, the second is 192.168.32.0/19.
theory.mask.title: Converting between prefix and mask
theory.mask.intro: A valid mask is a run of ones followed by a run of zeros. The prefix counts exactly those ones.
theory.mask.step1: Prefix to mask: every 8 ones make 255. If r bits are left over, that octet is 256 − 2^(8 − r), and the rest is 0.
theory.mask.step2: Mask to prefix: count the ones. Each 255 contributes 8, the interesting octet contributes what the table below shows.
theory.mask.step3: Only these octet values are valid: 255, 254, 252, 248, 240, 224, 192, 128, 0.
theory.mask.note: 255.255.255.160 is invalid: 160 is 10100000 in binary, so the ones are not in one run.
